newsitem.title: UK: N.Irish nationalists counter Protestant march plan.
newsitem.headline: N.Irish nationalists counter Protestant march plan.

text.p: Irish Roman Catholics said on Monday they would hold protests in Londonderry, Northern Ireland's second city, if a disputed pro-British Protestant parade went ahead in a sectarian flashpoint town next month.
A leading Protestant politician accused them of stoking up tension that is already growing over a traditionally turbulent Protestant "marching season" due to reach its climax in mid-July.
But Catholics pledged that their demonstrations in the nationalist stronghold of Londonderry would be peaceful.

Britain's Northern Ireland minister Mo Mowlam, launching a talks initiative with marchers and objectors, said she had no quick-fix solution to difficulties over the planned Protestant parade in Portadown town and other Catholic-inhabited areas.
But she made clear she was redoubling efforts to get a deal to defuse possible violence.
"I haven't got a magic wand...A lot has already been put on the table by others (and) so I don't have any ideal solution," Mowlam told BBC radio.
"What I do have is a determination to see what we can do to bring some kind of accommodation in the short time we have left."

A row over a Protestant parade through Portadown's Catholic Garvaghy Road enclave is fuelling fears of a repeat of turmoil last year when the province experienced more than a week of sectarian clashes and road blockades.

Donnacha Mac Niallais, a leader of the Bogside Residents Association in Londonderry, said the group was filing for police permission for parades in the city during July 6-12 to take place if Catholic objections to the Protestant parade in Portadown were ignored.

"If the parade is forced through Garvaghy Road, then emotions will be high, people will be seeking to do something," he told Reuters. "What we are going to do is channel that anger and emotion in a peaceful, non-violent way."
But Londonderry politician Gregory Campbell, of the pro-British Democratic Unionist Party, condemned the plan. "This is a deliberate attempt to raise the stakes," he told BBC radio.
Catholics in Garvaghy Road and elsewhere in the province were furious last year when police reversed a four-day ban and allowed Protestants to parade through.
Portadown Catholics plan to hold a street festival along the proposed route this year. Protestants say that that could trigger clashes.
Security analysts believe that police and government might decide to ban one or other of the events if there is no agreement beforehand.
